name: Zane Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the woks at Red Lantern, a pan-Asian place in the city centre with an open kitchen, so the customers watch us cook. There are three wok burners and I'm on the third, which is the junior one, mostly fried rice and noodles. I'm in at three to prep: slice the veg, marinate the chicken, make the sauce bases. Service till eleven, and we'll push out about four hundred dishes on a Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the flames and the noise, and the fact people film us. I'm still slow at tossing the heavy wok, the head wok chef, Lin, can do it one-handed and I need two. What wears me out is my wrists and the late finishes. On my days off I make short cooking videos, and I use AI every day to edit and plan them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly I'd be a bit surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is still a useful tool even if it's not a revolution. I'd post a video about how I use it to edit my clips and plan recipes. People like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing and slowly get better. I've got about nine months saved and some shares and a bit of crypto. If AI stays small, my real risk is my wrists giving out from tossing a heavy wok, not a computer taking my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking at Red Lantern, keep posting three videos a week, and keep putting money into shares. I'd ask Lin to teach me the one-handed toss by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Life's good if nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the videos bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred a month from ads and one sponsor, a knife company. It's small, but it's growing. AI does half the editing work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wrists, honestly. Cooks get injured. That's my real risk in a quiet world.

think: I keep improving at **Red Lantern** and growing slowly.

do: Learn the **one-handed toss** from Lin by summer next year.
feel: **Calm** and happy with life as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. That's what I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly. I'd make videos about how cooks can use AI for the boring parts, like allergen charts and costing. Practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. My kitchen job is hands-on, and the AI part makes my side business easier. Customers at my restaurant pay to watch real cooks throw flames, so a wok robot ruins the show before it saves any money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the channel, maybe hire a friend to help film. I'd learn every new AI editing tool. I'd keep the wok job because the videos need the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, Nadia, who works in a call centre. That's exactly the answering customers part. I'd help her find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you sure robots won't reach the woks soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are wok robots already, in some chains, they stir and pour. But Red Lantern sells the show, people come to watch people. That buys time.

I'd make videos on using AI for **allergen charts** and costing.
think: The change is **good for me** overall.
My **hands-on** job is safe while AI helps the channel.
The **open kitchen** show buys me time.
do: Grow the **channel** and hire a friend to film.

fieldNote: He believes the **open-kitchen show** protects his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Okay, that's fast. Robots by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy, and governments need a plan now. But I'd also say there'll be new kinds of work. I'd keep it practical on my channel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my wok job goes by 2031, show or no show. And the channel depends on ad money, which depends on people having jobs. My cooking channel lives on ad money, and ad money dries up when people lose their jobs, so AGI could hit my side income before my wok.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sell the crypto and keep cash. I'd push the channel hard for two years, build a name. Then maybe move into teaching cooking, classes for people with free time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is too much at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching cooking, why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if people lose jobs, they'll have time, and cooking is cheap entertainment. And a human teacher still matters, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a bit hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe. But hope is all I've got with two years. At least I've got savings to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-five when robots come. That's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so people should start now, not later. I'd make videos for cooks on how to plan a switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay. Five years is enough to turn my weekend cooking classes into a real business before any robot takes my wok station. I'd have time to build classes and the channel into a proper business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, start running small cooking classes on weekends. Grow the channel. Keep investing. Keep working woks until about 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to run the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, bookings, accounts, everything that isn't cooking. Saves me hiring an assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years she could retrain properly. I'd help her pay for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody should panic. I'd make content about long-term planning for cooks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do really well in this one. With ten years, I'd become a properly good wok cook first and then open a cooking school with my own name on the door. By then I want my own small cooking school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the wok job for three or four years, get really good. Build the channel and classes. Save up for a space around 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any doubts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether people still care about real cooks in 2039. I think they will, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lin, your head wok chef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start teaching, Lin. You're the best I've seen. People will pay to learn from you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Everything happens at once, and the channel and the job both get hit. I've got a wok job, a cooking channel and savings, and AGI in two years could still knock out all three. What would help is support for small businesses, like cheap loans, so people like me can build something new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side jobs. Lots of cooks have them, and they're how we'll get through this.

headlineQuote: I've got a wok job, a cooking channel and savings, and AGI in two years could still knock out all three.
portrait: Zane is a **junior wok cook** at Red Lantern, an open-kitchen pan-Asian restaurant.
He has **nine months saved**, shares, and a cooking video channel.
He uses **AI daily** and sees change as mostly good for him.
He stays **calm** in slow change but grows **anxious** with two years.
He'd build towards a **cooking school** with enough time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job and **channel** income both fall.
